Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Vision-language foundation models have enabled efficient adaptation to downstream tasks via prompt learning. However, real-world datasets frequently contain noisy labels. While prompt tuning is parameter-efficient, it remains vulnerable to overfitting when standard loss functions (such as Cross-Entropy) are applied to mislabeled data. Existing robust learning techniques often rely on complex architectures or slow training paradigms that negate the efficiency benefits of prompt learning. There is a critical need for a lightweight, robust prompt tuning framework that can inherently suppress the influence of label noise while leveraging the pre-aligned representation capabilities of foundation models.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the solution lies in a dual-strategy approach that harmonizes loss function robustness with geometric data purification.
1.  **Loss Robustness:** We hypothesize that Mean Absolute Error (MAE), despite its reputation for slow convergence in traditional deep learning, acts as a robust filter in the specific context of prompt learning. We believe MAE can suppress the gradient influence of noisy samples, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio during prompt updates.
2.  **Geometric Purification:** We postulate that the aligned latent space of vision-language models allows for effective "self-correction." By treating text features as prototypes in an Optimal Transport (OT) framework, we can identify and separate clean samples from noisy ones based on global distribution alignment rather than just local prediction confidence.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We aim to develop a framework named "NLPrompt" (Noise-Label Prompt Learning). The approach consists of three logical modules:

1.  **Prompt-Based Optimal Transport (Data Purification):**
    *   Instead of using randomly initialized prototypes for sample selection, we will leverage the text encoder of the foundation model.
    *   We will generate text features from class prompts and treat them as ground-truth prototypes.
    *   We will construct a cost matrix based on the similarity between image features and these text prototypes.
    *   By solving the Optimal Transport problem with marginal constraints, we will generate a global mapping (pseudo-labels) between images and classes. This mapping respects the global structure of the data better than per-sample confidence scores.

2.  **Dynamic Dataset Partitioning:**
    *   We will compare the OT-generated pseudo-labels against the provided dataset labels.
    *   Samples where the pseudo-label matches the given label will be categorized as the **Clean Subset**.
    *   Samples where there is a mismatch will be categorized as the **Noisy Subset**.

3.  **Hybrid Loss Optimization:**
    *   We will implement a split-stream training strategy to harmonize accuracy and robustness.
    *   **For the Clean Subset:** We will apply Cross-Entropy (CE) loss. Since these labels are verified by the OT process, CE will provide the necessary gradient sharpness for high accuracy and fast convergence.
    *   **For the Noisy Subset:** We will apply MAE loss. This ensures that the model learns from the visual features of these samples without being heavily penalized for their potentially incorrect labels, effectively preventing the prompt from overfitting to noise.

## Expected Contribution
We expect this project to provide a theoretical and practical framework for robust prompt learning. Theoretically, we aim to elucidate why MAE functions effectively as a noise-suppressor in the feature learning dynamics of prompt tuning. Practically, we intend to deliver a method that purifies data "on the fly" by exploiting the inherent alignment of vision-language models, eliminating the need for external noise-cleaning networks. This will allow for the deployment of foundation models on messy, real-world data without a significant drop in performance.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated the proposed method (NLPrompt) against state-of-the-art baselines on image classification tasks involving noisy labels.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Synthetic Noisy Datasets (7 total):** Caltech101, DTD (Describable Textures Dataset), EuroSAT, Flowers102, OxfordPets, StanfordCars, and UCF101.
    *   **Real-world Noisy Dataset:** Food101N.
    *   **Data Splits:** For synthetic datasets, we sampled a 16-shot training set (unless otherwise noted in few-shot analysis) and evaluated on the original test set.
    *   **Noise Injection (Synthetic):** We manually introduced label noise to the training sets.
        *   *Symmetric Noise (Sym):* Clean labels were randomly flipped to other labels with equal probability.
        *   *Asymmetric Noise (Asym):* Clean labels were flipped to a unique neighboring label (successor class).
        *   *Noise Rates:* 12.5%, 25.0%, 37.5%, 50.0%, 62.5%, and 75.0%.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   Top-1 Classification Accuracy (%) reported as the average of three runs with different seeds.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **CoOp:** Context Optimization (baseline prompt learning).
    *   **GCE:** CoOp trained with Generalized Cross Entropy loss (CoOp + GCE).
    *   **JoAPR:** Joint Adaptive Prompt and Prototype Refinement.
    *   **Prompt Tuning Variants (for generalization analysis):** VPT (Visual Prompt Tuning), MaPLe, and PromptSRC.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Model Backbone:** CLIP pre-trained model.
    *   **Image Encoder:** ResNet-50 (default for main results) and ViT-B/16 (used for ablation studies).
    *   **Text Encoder:** 63M parameter text transformer.
    *   **Prompt Configuration:** 16 shared context tokens across all categories; class token placed at the end.
    *   **Optimizer:** SGD with Cosine Annealing.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Initial learning rate of 0.002.
    *   **Training Duration:** 200 epochs (default); 100 epochs (ablation studies).
    *   **Hardware:** NVIDIA A40 GPU.
    *   **Purification Method (NLPrompt):** Used prompt-based Optimal Transport (PromptOT) to separate clean and noisy data. Applied Cross-Entropy (CE) loss to the clean subset and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) loss to the noisy subset.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Convergence Analysis (Caltech101):** We observed that as the noise level in the training data increased (0% to 75%), the performance of CoOp utilizing Cross-Entropy (CE) loss dropped significantly. Conversely, prompt learning utilizing Mean Absolute Error (MAE) loss exhibited negligible change in performance, maintaining high accuracy and fast convergence even under substantial noise.
*   **Methodology Framework:** We utilized text features from the vision-language model (CLIP) as prototypes to construct an optimal transport (OT) matrix. We observed that this matrix effectively partitioned the dataset into clean and noisy subsets. This allowed for a dual-loss strategy: applying CE loss to the clean subset and MAE loss to the noisy subset.
*   **Few-Shot Robustness:** We analyzed the effect of shot count (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) on accuracy under noisy conditions (50% noise). We observed that while all methods improved with more shots, our method consistently outperformed the baseline (CoOp) across all shot numbers on Caltech101, DTD, UCF101, and Flowers102.
*   **Generalization Capabilities:** We observed that our method acts as a general framework that can be integrated with other prompt-tuning methods (VPT, MaPLe, PromptSRC). In all tested cases, adding our method improved the baseline performance of these techniques under noisy conditions.
*   **Ablation Findings:**
    *   Using MAE alone (PromptMAE) outperformed using CE alone in noisy settings.
    *   Text feature initialization for the OT process yielded higher performance than random initialization.
    *   The dual-strategy (NLPrompt) of using purified data (CE on clean, MAE on noisy) outperformed removing the noisy data entirely or removing the clean data entirely.
    *   NLPrompt achieved the best performance across all tested noise ratios in the ablation study compared to the individual components.

Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs

• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Vision-language foundation models (VLMs) typically rely on prompt learning to adapt to downstream tasks. While effective, this paradigm assumes high-quality supervision. In real-world applications, annotated datasets inevitably contain noisy labels. Standard prompt tuning methods utilize Cross-Entropy (CE) loss, which is prone to overfitting these noisy labels, thereby degrading the generalizability of the learned prompts.

While Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is theoretically recognized for robustness against noise, it is historically underutilized in classification tasks due to slow convergence and suboptimal performance on clean data. Furthermore, existing data purification techniques, such as those based on Optimal Transport (OT), typically rely on randomly initialized prototypes to estimate clean labels. This standard OT approach fails to leverage the intrinsic semantic alignment already present in pre-trained VLMs, leading to inefficient noise filtering in the context of prompt learning. We require a robust framework that specifically adapts prompt learning to noisy environments by rethinking the loss landscape and the initialization of data purification mechanisms.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose **NLPrompt**, a noise-label prompt learning framework. Our hypothesis consists of two distinct components:

1.  **PromptMAE:** We posit that within the specific dynamics of prompt learning, the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) loss acts as a natural noise filter. Unlike traditional deep learning contexts, we hypothesize that MAE in prompt tuning suppresses the gradient influence of noisy samples—categorized as "task-irrelevant" features—thereby enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio during optimization.
2.  **PromptOT:** We hypothesize that the alignment between image and text encoders in VLMs can be exploited to initialize Optimal Transport. By using text features generated by prompts as prototypes (rather than random initialization), we can construct a more accurate transportation matrix to identify and separate clean samples from noisy ones.

By combining these, we will effectively partition data and apply a hybrid loss strategy: high-precision CE for clean data and robust MAE for noisy data.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will implement a framework that harmonizes robust loss functions with a geometry-aware data purification mechanism.

### 1. Preliminaries and Prompt Learning Formulation
We consider a classification task with $C$ classes. Let $g$ be the pre-trained image encoder and $h$ be the pre-trained text encoder.
For an input image $\mathbf{x}$, we obtain the image feature $\mathbf{g} = g(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^m$.
We will introduce a learnable prompt $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a fixed class-specific prompt $\mathbf{p}_c \in \{\mathbf{p}_1, \dots, \mathbf{p}_C\}$. The text feature for class $c$ is generated as:
$$ \mathbf{h}_c = h(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{p}_c) \in \mathbb{R}^m $$

We define the prediction probability $\mathbf{s}_i$ for an image $\mathbf{x}_i$ via the softmax of cosine similarity:
$$ s_i(\mathbf{p}) = \mathrm{SOFTMAX}(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{h})) $$

### 2. PromptOT: Optimal Transport for Data Purification
To separate clean data from noisy data, we will design a **Prompt-based Optimal Transport (PromptOT)** mechanism. Unlike standard methods, we will strictly avoid random prototype initialization.

**Cost Matrix Construction:**
We will utilize the pre-trained CLIP text embeddings as prototypes.
Let $\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ be the image feature matrix for a batch of $N$ images.
Let $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times d}$ be the text feature matrix generated by the current prompts.
We compute the cost matrix $\mathbf{C}_{cost}$ as the negative logarithm of the similarity:
$$ \mathbf{C}_{cost} = -\log(\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{I}^\top) $$

**OT Formulation:**
We formulate the transport problem to find the optimal coupling matrix $\mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{C \times N}$ that maps images to class prototypes. We will solve the following entropy-regularized optimization problem:
$$ \begin{array}{rl} {\underset{\mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{C \times N}}{\operatorname*{min}}} & {\langle -\log(\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{I}^\top), \mathbf{Q} \rangle} \\ {\mathrm{s.t.}} & {\mathbf{Q} \mathbb{1}_N = \frac{1}{C} \mathbb{1}_C, \quad \mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbb{1}_C = \frac{1}{N} \mathbb{1}_N} \end{array} $$
where $\mathbb{1}$ represents a vector of ones, enforcing uniform marginal distributions.

**Pseudo-Label Generation:**
Upon solving for the optimal matrix $\mathbf{Q}^\star$, we will derive the pseudo-label $\tilde{y}_i$ for the $i$-th image by identifying the maximum transport probability:
$$ \tilde{y}_i = \arg\max_j \mathbf{Q}_{ij}^\star $$

### 3. Dataset Partitioning
Using the derived pseudo-labels $\tilde{y}$, we will partition the training batch into two subsets by comparing the pseudo-label against the given (potentially noisy) ground truth label $\hat{y}_i$:
*   **Clean Subset ($\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{clean}}$):** Samples where $\hat{y}_i = \tilde{y}_i$.
*   **Noisy Subset ($\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{noisy}}$):** Samples where $\hat{y}_i \neq \tilde{y}_i$.

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{clean}} = \{ i \mid \hat{y}_i = \tilde{y}_i \}, \quad \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{noisy}} = \{ j \mid \hat{y}_j \neq \tilde{y}_j \} $$

### 4. Harmonized Optimization Objective
We will train the learnable prompt $\mathbf{p}$ using a hybrid loss function that applies Cross-Entropy (CE) to the clean subset (for convergence speed and accuracy) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) to the noisy subset (for robustness).

The total loss $\ell_{\mathrm{NLPrompt}}$ is defined as:
$$ \ell_{\mathrm{NLPrompt}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{clean}}} -\mathbf{y}_i^\top \log \mathbf{s}_i + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{noisy}}} ||\mathbf{y}_j - \mathbf{s}_j||_1 $$
where $\mathbf{y}_i$ is the one-hot target vector and $\mathbf{s}_i$ is the predicted similarity vector.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Theoretical Robustness Analysis:** We intend to provide a theoretical analysis based on feature learning theory to demonstrate *why* MAE is effective in prompt learning. We expect to show that MAE facilitates the dominance of task-relevant features over task-irrelevant (noise) coefficients during gradient descent.
2.  **Novel Purification Initialization:** We will demonstrate that initializing Optimal Transport with VLM text features—rather than random vectors—significantly improves the accuracy of pseudo-label generation in zero-shot or few-shot noisy settings.
3.  **Unified Framework:** The NLPrompt architecture will serve as a general-purpose, robust solution for vision-language adaptation, effectively mitigating the trade-off between noise robustness and convergence speed.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
